## Overview

`add` in `calc.js` returns `a + b` with no coercion and no type check. JavaScript's `+` is overloaded, so two numeric strings concatenate instead of adding. `add("2", "3")` returns the string `"23"`, not the number `5`.

The whole function, read from `/private/var/folders/11/m_kwnqr97632l_cjt0mhytvh0000gn/T/pstack-live-93ULKL/work/calc.js`:

```js
export function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
```

## How It Works

`+` adds numbers only when both operands are numbers. One string operand is enough to switch it to string concatenation, and `add` never inspects or converts its arguments. Observed on this machine with Node, run by me:

| Call | Result | `typeof` result |
|---|---|---|
| `add("2", "3")` | `"23"` | `"string"` |
| `add("2", 3)` | `"23"` | `"string"` |
| `add(2, 3)` | `5` | `"number"` |

```
{"r1":"23","t1":"string","r2":"23","t2":"string","r3":5,"t3":"number"}
```

The mixed call matters as much as the two-string case. A caller that reads one operand from a text input and passes the other as a literal still gets concatenation.

## Where Things Live

The repo holds a single file, `calc.js`, which exports `add`. Git has one commit on it, `42a371d "calc"`, which added the file in this form, so no earlier version coerced to numbers. No caller and no test exists anywhere in the repo, so the behavior is unexercised today. Anything that imports `add` inherits the concatenation.

## Gotchas

The parameter names `a` and `b` are generic and carry no numeric intent. The function name does. That mismatch between the name `add` and what `+` actually does is the entire bug surface.

The function never checks `typeof` and never calls `Number(...)` or `parseInt(...)`. If numeric strings are a real input, the caller has to convert, because `add` will not.
